title: The Leafy Greens in Your Thali May Be Quietly Protecting Your Lungs — and a Major New Study Shows How
excerpt: Researchers tracked 179,000 adults for over a decade and found that those who ate the most vitamin K1 — abundant in spinach, kale, and methi — had a 16% lower risk of chronic lung disease.
body:
India's culinary tradition has always placed leafy greens at the centre of the plate — from the palak paneer of the north to the keerai kootu of the south. Now, a large-scale study suggests that tradition may carry an underappreciated medical benefit: protection against one of the world's deadliest lung diseases.

Researchers at Australia's Edith Cowan University analysed data from 179,062 participants in the UK Biobank over a 10-and-a-half-year period and found a clear link between dietary vitamin K1 intake and lung health. Their findings, published in *The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, showed that participants who consumed the most vitamin K1 had a **16% lower risk of developing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)** compared to those who consumed the least. They also had measurably better lung function — their lungs could hold and move more air, a critical factor in maintaining quality of life with age.

COPD, which includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis, is the third leading cause of death worldwide, responsible for roughly 4 million deaths annually. While smoking remains the dominant risk factor, the disease also strikes non-smokers — particularly those exposed to air pollution, occupational dust, and indoor cooking fumes, conditions disproportionately common in South Asia.

## How Vitamin K1 May Shield the Lungs

The researchers believe vitamin K1 helps protect the tiny elastic fibres inside the lungs — the structures that allow them to stretch during inhalation and spring back during exhalation. When these fibres degrade, breathing gradually becomes more laboured. Vitamin K1 appears to help preserve their flexibility through its role in activating Matrix Gla Protein (MGP), a calcium-regulatory protein that prevents the calcification of soft tissues, including lung elastin.

"Eating more leafy greens is a simple step that could help support lung health over time," said Dr. Chengfeng Li, the study's lead author. "But a healthy diet plays a supporting role — it won't cancel out smoking."

Interestingly, vitamin K2 — found in fermented foods, eggs, and certain dairy products — did not show the same protective effect against COPD, though moderate amounts were linked to marginally better lung function. The researchers speculate that the difference may be partly explained by context: K1-rich leafy greens come bundled with fibre, antioxidants, and other micronutrients that may work synergistically, while K2-rich foods are often consumed alongside processed or red meats that carry their own health burdens.

## The Indian Greens Advantage

For diaspora families who grew up eating traditional Indian food, this study is quietly validating. Indian cuisine features an extraordinary diversity of leafy greens — many of which are among the richest dietary sources of vitamin K1 on the planet.

A single cup of cooked palak (spinach) delivers roughly 888 micrograms of vitamin K1 — more than seven times the recommended daily intake. Sarson ka saag (mustard greens), methi (fenugreek leaves), bathua (lamb's quarters), and amaranth leaves are similarly potent. Even the humble curry leaf, tossed into a tempering pan almost as an afterthought, carries meaningful K1 content.

The challenge for NRIs is that emigration often means a dietary shift away from these greens. Busy weeknight meals in the US, UK, or Canada tend to drift toward convenience — and convenience rarely means a plate of methi thepla or kootu. The data suggests that maintaining, or reintroducing, these traditional greens into the weekly rotation is worth the effort — not just for the familiar taste, but for measurable lung protection.

## Air Quality Adds Urgency

The study's findings carry particular weight for the diaspora because of the air quality crisis in India. Millions of NRIs have parents and relatives living in cities where PM2.5 levels routinely exceed WHO guidelines by 10 to 15 times. COPD rates in India are among the highest globally, and household air pollution from cooking with solid fuels remains a major contributor, especially for women in rural areas.

While the UK Biobank cohort does not directly represent Indian populations, the biological mechanism — K1's role in preserving lung elastin — is universal. And the dietary intervention is among the simplest in preventive medicine: eat more greens.

## What This Means for You

The study does not prove causation — it is observational — and no single nutrient is a substitute for avoiding tobacco, reducing pollution exposure, or treating existing lung disease. But the 16% risk reduction is meaningful, especially over a lifetime of consistent intake. Previous research has also linked adequate vitamin K consumption to lower rates of emphysema and better lung function in otherwise healthy adults.

For diaspora families — especially those with parents or grandparents in pollution-heavy Indian cities — the practical takeaway is straightforward. The palak, the methi, the sarson ka saag that already anchors so many meals is doing more than satisfying a craving for home. It may be keeping lungs flexible, resilient, and working well into old age.

*The study, "Dietary vitamin K intakes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, adult asthma, and lung function: a prospective cohort study in the UK Biobank," was published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in June 2026.*
